$comment: The shared contract: what every SDK puts on the wire, beyond the body itself.
A change here is a change to every SDK. Each target reads this file from its own suite, sends a
real request to a listening socket and holds what arrived against the list below, so a header
dropped or renamed in one target fails there rather than at the first API that notices.
Header names are matched without regard to case, as HTTP compares them.
A value is a template: `${name}` is a hole and everything around it is literal. A suite fills
the holes it can speak for — `${token}` is the credential the client was built with, and
`${language}` is the target reading the file — and what is left over is a hole no suite can fill
without reimplementing the client it is testing. Those are matched rather than compared: the
literal text has to arrive in order, anchored at both ends, with something non-empty in each
hole. A template whose holes are all filled is an exact string, which is what the first three
below are, so nothing about how they are checked has changed.
`max_composed_bytes` bounds any value a client composes rather than repeats — one carrying a
hole no suite fills, which is one built out of what the platform said rather than out of what
is written here. Those parts are as long as the platform feels like making them, so a client
cuts them to fit rather than sending whatever it was handed.
`when` says which requests carry the header, and is one of the `occasions` below.
This is the smallest thing worth pinning and the easiest to let drift: a client that omits the
representation it accepts works perfectly until the API serves a second one.
`Hook0-Client-Options` reuses the grammar of `X-Hook0-Signature` rather than inventing a
second one: parts joined by `,`, each part cut at its FIRST `=`, so a value containing `=`
stays whole. Every client already emits and reads that shape, so this header costs no new
parser and offers no new way to get parsing wrong.
Its four parts are the retry policy the client was built with, in this fixed order, each an
integer with no unit suffix and every duration in milliseconds. Fixed order is what lets a
suite compare the whole value as one string instead of parsing it back apart.
It reports the policy IN FORCE, not what this particular send did with it. A policy allowing
four attempts says `attempts=4` on a send that succeeded on the first, because four is what it
would have allowed; and a policy allowing one still states the delays it holds, because they
are what it holds, and a reader seeing `attempts=1` already knows none will be waited.
In force also means AFTER the client's own clamps. A client asked for a thousand attempts and
capped at sixteen states sixteen, because sixteen is what its traffic will show and a thousand
would send a reader looking for a burst that cannot happen. This is the one place the two
readings of `configured` come apart, and getting it wrong in one target puts two Hook0 SDKs on
the wire describing the same setup differently.

headers.name: Authorization
headers.reason: the credential the API authenticates the application with

headers.name: Accept
headers.reason: the representation every SDK is written to read; a client that asks for nothing is at the mercy of whatever the API decides to serve the day it serves more than one

headers.name: Content-Type
headers.reason: what the body is written as, which a request carrying no body has nothing to declare

headers.name: User-Agent
headers.reason: which SDK, at which version, on which runtime and operating system, is talking to the API; an instance can otherwise not tell a deprecation that has reached everybody from one that has reached nobody, and nothing can go back and ask a client that shipped two years ago

headers.name: Hook0-Client-Options
headers.reason: the retry policy behind the request, which is the only client setting the API can see the consequences of without being told: a burst of identical requests arriving inside a few seconds is a client repeating one send, and without this header it is indistinguishable from a client in a loop. It also makes the far commoner mistake legible — a client left at one attempt reports a flaky API for failures a single retry would have absorbed, and nothing on the API side can tell that today
